title: The tax collector's table (Matthew 9:9–13)
hookLine: Matthew is called from his booth and throws a dinner full of the wrong people

lines: THE LEAST POPULAR JOB IN TOWN.
cards: Think of the least popular job in your town. The person who tows your car. The one who sends the final notice.
Now make it worse: this person works for the occupying power, and everyone assumes they skim a little extra for themselves. That was a tax collector in Galilee.
In Capernaum there was a toll booth, and in it sat a man named Matthew. People crossed the street to avoid him. Pious people wouldn't eat with him.
One day Jesus walks past the booth, stops, looks at him, and says two words.

teach.h: FOLLOW ME. HE AROSE AND FOLLOWED.
teach.b: The two words: "Follow me." The Gospel that carries his name says simply: "And he arose up and followed him." No speech, no conditions.
He gets up from the money and goes. Mark and Luke tell the same story and call him Levi.

teach.h: A DINNER FULL OF THE WRONG PEOPLE.
teach.b: Then comes the dinner. Jesus sits at table in the house, and many tax collectors and sinners come and eat with him and his disciples. Matthew has invited everyone he knows, and everyone he knows is the wrong crowd.
Some Pharisees, who took holiness very seriously, ask the disciples: why does your master eat with tax collectors and sinners? In that world, sharing a table meant sharing a life.
Jesus answers with a picture from medicine: "They that are in health need not a physician, but they that are ill." Then he sends them to the prophet Hosea: "I will have mercy and not sacrifice."
A doctor who avoids sick people isn't much of a doctor. He came for the ones who know they need help. Catholics keep Matthew's feast on September twenty-first.
In Rome, a well-known Caravaggio painting catches this moment: a beam of light across a dark counting table, and a man pointing at himself, as if to say, me?
And Pope Francis took his motto from an old homily by Saint Bede about this scene. In Latin: miserando atque eligendo.

teach.h: BY HAVING MERCY, AND BY CHOOSING.
teach.b: Roughly, by having mercy, and by choosing.

teach.h: I WILL HAVE MERCY AND NOT SACRIFICE.
teach.b: He looked at Matthew with mercy, and chose him.

how: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Matthew, apostle and evangelist, on September 21, when this Gospel is read at Mass; Pope Francis's episcopal motto, miserando atque eligendo, comes from Saint Bede's homily on it.

games.why: many tax collectors and sinners sit down to eat with Jesus. when questioned, he says the sick are the ones who need a doctor.

practice: Think of someone outside your usual circle, the coworker nobody talks to, the neighbor you nod at, the relative the family whispers about, and picture sitting across a table from them.
Notice what rises in you: awkwardness, judgment, maybe curiosity. Then picture the look Jesus gave Matthew, and imagine being looked at that way yourself; if you pray, you can ask for that look.

wordCard.voice: publican. The old word for a tax collector, the job Matthew left behind the moment Jesus said follow me.

orig.note: Greek: a toll or tax collector, the job Matthew left. The old English Bibles say publican.

carryVoice: Your line: he came for the sick. The doctor goes where the sick are. That's day thirty-seven.
